entries.title: Goldberg-Variationen
entries.about: Bach published it in 1741 as the fourth part of his Clavier-Übung (keyboard practice): an aria, thirty variations on its bass line, and the aria again. Every third variation is a canon, each at a wider interval than the last. The story that it was written for the harpsichordist Johann Gottlieb Goldberg to play to a count who could not sleep comes from Bach's first biographer and is doubted.

entries.about: Beethoven called it Sonata quasi una fantasia, a sonata in the manner of a fantasy, because it opens with a slow movement instead of a fast one. entries.about: Für Elise was never published in Beethoven's lifetime. The scholar Ludwig Nohl printed it in 1867 from an autograph that has since been lost, so no one can check how he read the dedication. Who Elise was is still debated: one theory is that Nohl misread “Therese”, for Therese Malfatti, whom Beethoven hoped to marry around 1810.

entries.title: Prelude in D-flat major
alt: Prélude no. 15 in D‐flat major, op. 28 Raindrop: Sostenuto
entries.about: The nickname isn't Chopin's. It comes from George Sand's memoir of the winter of 1838–39, which the two spent in a former monastery at Valldemossa on Majorca. She describes coming home through a storm to find him playing a prelude he had just written, convinced he had dreamed of drowning while drops of water fell on his chest. Which prelude she meant is uncertain, but the A♭ that repeats through this one, written as G♯ in its dark middle section, kept the name here.
